summary:
The “Dancing with SARs” challenge aims to develop an interactive application using satellite radar data. It is based on the NASA-ISRO NISAR mission.
ChangeSignal Global is a geospatial environmental monitoring platform, accessible from a browser or phone as a progressive web app. It locates ecosystems, obtains satellite data, assesses changes and presents results backed by verifiable sources, using radar and remote sensing, including the NASA-ISRO NISAR mission.
It has two indicators: ICH, for wetlands and peatlands, and ICC, for coastlines and tributaries. A four-state traffic light (green, yellow, red and gray "not assessed") avoids inventing scores: if data are missing or the methodology is not validated, the system says so and explains why.
Its impact aims to anticipate damage to ecosystems that regulate water, store carbon and sustain communities. The pilot area is the province of Chiloé, with 183,915 inhabitants and documented water problems. It offers early warning, better-informed management decisions and the ability to scale to other territories and ecosystems.
It declares its limits: the NISAR data series is short, so it relies on other sensors, and building the application is not the same as scientifically validating the indicators.
It is creative in its honesty, its common language, its use of radar to see through clouds, its traceable evidence and its modular architecture. The team prioritized scientific rigor, low cost, ethics and feasibility.
details:
I. What is it and how does it work?

ChangeSignal Global is a geospatial environmental monitoring platform, accessible from a browser or phone as a progressive web app (PWA). It is not just a world map with markers: it locates ecosystems, retrieves geographic information, obtains satellite data, assesses environmental change, and presents results backed by verifiable sources. It uses radar and other remote sensing data, including the NASA-ISRO NISAR mission, as the challenge requires.

Two indicators :

  • ICH (Wetlands & Peatlands): assesses wetlands and peatlands.
  • ICC (Coastline & Tributaries): assesses coastlines and tributaries.

Four-state traffic light :

  • Green: Good condition.
  • Yellow: Warning.
  • Red: Critical.
  • Gray: Not assessed. There is not enough evidence or methodology.

Design principle : no artificial scores are generated. When data are missing or the methodology is not validated, the system responds “not assessed” and explains why. The green, yellow and red thresholds come from a scientific methodology defined and validated from the radar data.

Each result reports : score (if applicable), status, assessment date, variables used, sources, data resolution, quality and coverage, methodological confidence (if a defined model exists), and reasons for an incomplete assessment.

Screens:

  • Home: summary of activity, indicators, latest assessments and alerts.
  • Explore: world map with toggleable layers (wetlands, peatlands, Ramsar sites, WHSRN sites, mangroves, coastlines and user-drawn areas), place search, point or polygon selection, and an environmental assessment sheet.
  • Reports: previous assessments, period comparison, and downloadable reports in CSV, GeoJSON and PDF.

Assessment flow:

  • The user selects a point or draws an area (for example, a coast of Chiloé).
  • The application sends the geometry to the server.
  • The geographic module queries the database and recognizes the ecosystems present.
  • Environmental inventories are consulted, and the system checks whether suitable satellite data exist.
  • If sufficient data and methodology exist, the data are clipped and processed, the variables are calculated and compared with earlier periods.
  • Evidence and results are saved, and the application displays the environmental sheet with its traffic light.

Variables that can be analyzed.

  • NDVI, NDWI and MNDWI (vegetation and water),
  • SAR backscatter,
  • Water extent,
  • Vegetation cover
  • Temporal change.

A satellite index does not by itself amount to an ecological assessment: a change in NDVI, for example, does not prove wetland degradation. Seasonality, acquisition conditions and field observations are taken into account.

Reference architecture.

  • Frontend (PWA). Function: map, layers, sheets and reports. Reference technologies: React, TypeScript, Vite, MapLibre GL, Turf.js.
  • Backend (API). Function: geographic queries, assessments, reports and alerts. Reference technologies: Python, FastAPI.
  • Database. Function: sites, geometries, assessments, evidence and history. Reference technologies: PostgreSQL with PostGIS.
  • Environmental data. Function: satellite catalogs and ecosystem inventories. Reference technologies: STAC, Sentinel, Landsat, NISAR, Ramsar, WHSRN.
  • Processing engine. Function: satellite processing and calculation of ICH and ICC. Reference technologies: GDAL, Rasterio, GeoPandas, NumPy, Xarray.
  • Results. Function: traffic lights, assessments, alerts, reports and exports. Formats: CSV, GeoJSON, PDF.
  • Status of the deployed version (confirmed) or (to be confirmed). For each layer, indicate whether it is implemented, partial or planned:
  • Web application with interactive map and sheets: Confirmed
  • ICH and ICC traffic lights with “not assessed” status: Confirmed
  • Real NISAR data loaded (scenes and dates): Confirmed
  • Sentinel-1, Sentinel-2 or Landsat data: Confirmed
  • Inventories (wetlands, peatlands, Ramsar, WHSRN): Confirmed
  • Reports and exports: Confirmed
  • Public link to the application: Confirmed

II. Expected impact and benefits

Problem. Wetlands, peatlands, coasts and tributaries regulate water, store carbon and sustain communities, but their changes are usually noticed when they are already hard to reverse, and the necessary information is scattered across many inventories and catalogs.

In Chiloé there are concrete signs. In 2018 the health authority restricted water consumption in parts of the city of Queilén because of high chloride levels, and the communal dialogues of the Regional Government of Los Lagos (2023) record problems of water supply and availability in several communes of the province of Chiloé and the region.

Expected benefits.

  • One place to locate ecosystems, view their information and assess their change, with sources visible.
  • Early warning to prioritize where to inspect before damage becomes irreversible.
  • More informed environmental management decisions for municipalities, coastal border administration agencies and water services.
  • Scientific transparency: the “not assessed” status avoids presenting results that cannot be justified.
  • Education and citizen science: explaining with real cases how the Earth and its ecosystems are observed from space.
  • Scalability: start in Chiloé and expand to other territories in Chile and the world, as well as to other ecosystems such as mangroves and estuaries.
  • Scale of the pilot area. According to INE projections for 2024, the province of Chiloé has 183,915 in habitants. [confirmed at ine.gob.cl]

Limits we declare.

Calibrated NISAR data have been public since July 20, 2026 for observations since June 17, 2026, so its own time series is short; the baseline must rely on other sensors, which are identified on screen.

Building the application is not the same as scientific validation: ICH and ICC only deliver scores when their methodologies, variables, thresholds and criteria are defined and validated. [Validation status confirmed]

A detected change indicates where to look first; it does not identify or accuse anyone responsible.

III. Tools, languages, software and hardware

  • Creation and deployment: Google AI Studio. Used according to the team. [Gemini model and deployment mode confirmed]
  • Application languages: TypeScript, JavaScript, HTML and CSS. Reference. [Languages actually generated confirmed]
  • Frontend: React, Vite, MapLibre GL, Turf.js, PWA. Reference. [Confirmed]
  • Backend: Python and FastAPI. Reference. [Confirmed]
  • Geographic database: PostgreSQL with PostGIS, GiST indexes. Reference. [Confirmed]
  • Satellite processing: GDAL, Rasterio, GeoPandas, Shapely, NumPy, Xarray, TiTiler, STAC. Reference. [Confirmed]
  • Data formats: GeoJSON, GeoPackage, COG (Cloud Optimized GeoTIFF), vector tiles when volume grows. Reference.
  • Heavy tasks: task queue with Redis and Celery. Planned; to be added when processes justify it.
  • NISAR data access: Python script (asf_search, h5py, NumPy, pandas, Pillow). Written without network access. [Confirmed]
  • Local development: Linux Mint, Visual Studio Code, Git and GitHub, Docker and Docker Compose, QGIS. Reference. [Confirmed]
  • Publishing: GitHub [Confirmed]
  • AI assistance: Google AI Studio and Claude (Anthropic). Claude was used for planning, Spanish-to-English translation of reports, an interface prototype and a support script. [Confirmed]
  • Hardware: personal computers and phones with a browser. No special hardware is required. [Confirmed]

IV. In what sense is it creative?

  • Honesty as a product feature. The fourth state, “not assessed,” makes visible what is not known instead of filling it with fictitious numbers.
  • A common language for everyone. The same traffic light and the same sheets work for a wetland in Chiloé, a mangrove or an estuary on another continent.
  • Two indicators, two stories. ICH tells the story of wetlands and peatlands; ICC that of the coastal edge and its tributaries; together they show how they relate within a basin.
  • Radar to see through clouds. SAR and NISAR’s L-band make it possible to observe areas with almost permanent cloud cover, such as southern Chile.
  • Traceable evidence. Each result shows where it comes from: source, date, resolution, quality and limitations.
  • From map to action. Users can draw their own area, compare periods and download a report.
  • Modular architecture. Each source has its own connector, so if one service fails the rest keep working, and each indicator is an independent module.

V. Factors considered as a team

  • Scientific rigor over appearance. The most important decision was not to confuse building the application with validating the assessment system: the map, database and interface can be built from the start, but ICH and ICC only deliver scores once validated.
  • Honesty about the data. NISAR’s temporal coverage is declared and complementary sensors are identified.
  • Traceability. The download date, version, geographic coverage, license, resolution, methodology and limitations of each dataset are recorded.
  • Modularity and resilience. Independent connectors per source and separate modules for each indicator.
  • Low cost and open source. Free or open tools and public data.
  • Start local and scale. Validate in Chiloé before processing large volumes, then expand to other territories.
  • Appropriate storage for each data type. Geometries in PostGIS, images in object storage as COGs, and no satellite images stored inside the database.
  • Performance on a world map. The browser only requests data for the visible region and zoom level.
  • Accessibility and phone use. Installable PWA and traffic-light language.
  • Ethics and respect. No accusing people or companies; no stigmatizing localities; careful handling of local information.
  • Feasibility within the hackathon timeframe. Prioritized, complementary build stages.

Team Naour Group : Claudio Naour López, Verónica Cheuquepil Ojeda, Trinidad Naour Cheuquepil. Chiloé Island, Chile. Challenge: Dancing with the SAR
